deck.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after Trump says he 'made the deal'
deck.sub: Less than two weeks after his resignation over an alleged Chinese spy, the board brings Huang back, citing US government input; shares jump 31%.
deck.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, less than two weeks after he resigned over an affair with a woman US officials call a Chinese spy. The board says US government officials gave input; Trump says he made the deal. Shares jumped 31.5%. The board's investigation continues.
deck.whyItMatters: The leadership crisis is over but the open questions are not: the SEC accounting probe, the delayed 10-Q and Megaspeed all remain, now with the White House visibly involved in a private board's decision.
deck.update: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, citing input from senior US government officials; Trump says he 'made the deal'; shares jump 31.5%
deck.checked: Checked on Nvidia's press release and the BBC (both opened); share price from market data
deck.detailHtml:
Nvidia's board voted unanimously on 23 Nov to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board member 'effective immediately', after meetings in which it was 'satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead' (Nvidia release). The board says it 'received input from senior levels of the United States government' and is confident his return 'poses no national security risk'. Huang resigned on 12 Nov after reports of affairs, including with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive US officials believe worked for Chinese intelligence; only last Tuesday the board said it did not intend to reinstate him (BBC). Trump said he 'convinced' the board and 'made the deal'. The independent directors' investigation 'will proceed to conclusion', and a new National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors will oversee trade compliance. Interim CEO Colette Kress stays CFO; Harvey Jones remains chair. Democrats accuse the administration of trading national security for market gains; Huang is due to testify to Congress in early December. Shares closed up 31.5% at $165.05.

The board's statement is unusual: it says outright that US government officials gave it input and that, on that basis, it is satisfied Huang poses no national-security risk. Six days earlier the same board had said it would not bring him back. Trump said on Monday that he had persuaded the board; Democrats, including Elizabeth Warren, want Congress to act, and Foreign Policy called it the biggest national-security scandal in US history.

Markets voted the other way. Nvidia added close to $1tn in value and took the Nasdaq up 6.5% (see the markets card). But the issues that drove last week's fall are still there: the SEC's reported look at Nvidia's accounting, the delayed quarterly filing, about $104bn of 2025 revenue booked through Singapore, and Megaspeed, which Commerce moved to blacklist the same day. The board's investigation continues, and a new committee will watch export compliance.

deck.headline: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler for $43.9bn, the biggest cybersecurity deal ever
deck.summary: CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9bn, a 34% premium and the largest cybersecurity takeover ever. It joins device and cloud protection with Zscaler's zero-trust network security. CrowdStrike shares fell about 9%; closing is expected in the second half of its fiscal 2028.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks that buy endpoint and zero-trust network security from these two vendors face a single supplier for both within about a year; review contract terms, exit clauses and concentration risk now.
deck.checked: Deal terms checked in CrowdStrike's SEC 8-K exhibit and SiliconANGLE's report (opened); share moves from market data
deck.storyline: Storyline: the AI security business · day 7
deck.detailHtml: CrowdStrike said on 23 Nov it will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal that values it at about $43.9bn, or $260.40 a share, a 34% premium to Friday's close; Zscaler holders get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares each (CrowdStrike SEC filing). It is the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record. CrowdStrike's Falcon protects devices and cloud workloads; Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange protects the network connections between them, a market CrowdStrike calls cybersecurity's largest. CrowdStrike expects about $1bn of revenue synergies and $500m of cost savings. Closing is expected in the second half of its fiscal year ending January 2028, subject to Zscaler shareholder and regulatory approval; Zscaler owes a $1.4bn break fee in some cases. Investors were cool: CrowdStrike fell about 9% to $208.97 and Zscaler rose about 18% to $229.24 (market data).

deck.headline: OpenRouter drops three AI providers after decoy prompts leaked to attackers
deck.summary: OpenRouter removed Together AI, Phala and Novita and stripped zero-retention status from 125 endpoints after Dragos showed decoy credentials hidden in test prompts were stolen and used by outsiders. Dragos sent about two million prompts over five months. OpenRouter says its own systems were not breached.
deck.whyItMatters: A 'zero retention' label on a model router is only as good as the hosts behind it; any bank sending customer or code data through third-party inference should map which providers actually serve its requests and assume secrets in prompts can leak.
deck.checked: Checked on Dragos's own write-up and BleepingComputer's report (both opened); provider statements not opened
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks through software and vendors · day 9
deck.detailHtml: Model marketplace OpenRouter removed three inference providers, Together AI, Phala and Novita, on 23 Nov and revoked zero-data-retention (ZDR) eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution, BleepingComputer reports. The trigger was a five-month test by industrial-security firm Dragos, which sent about two million prompts containing unique links and decoy credentials through widely used AI services. Dragos says data from at least three providers was exposed: its seeded prompts were later used to try to get into its test systems and canary AWS accounts. It also found resellers able to view and keep customer prompts with standard logging, and providers not honouring privacy settings. OpenRouter says its own systems were not breached. Atlas Cloud withdrew its models pending security testing; Together AI said an AI coding agent had exposed data.
deck.sourcesHtml: OFFICIALDragos: Three breaches, endless leaks: your AI supply chain needs canariesREPORTINGBleepingComputer: OpenRouter drops AI providers over leaked prompts and secrets · The Hacker News: OpenRouter drops 3 providers after prompt theft

deck.headline: Azure API Management flaw exploited to steal customers' stored keys and secrets
deck.summary: Microsoft says attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to read stored secrets, including client secrets and subscription keys, on instances not set up to its best practices. It found the bug on 18 Nov and mitigated it a day later. Norway links it to attacks on energy firms.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks publish many internal and partner APIs through APIM; if you run Classic tiers, rotate every stored secret and client credential now and check logs back to before 18 Nov.
deck.storyline: Storyline: when one cloud fails · day 7
deck.detailHtml: Microsoft told customers in an Azure Service Health advisory (MZK9-GH0) that a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal credentials stored in the service, BleepingComputer reports (23 Nov). Microsoft says it found the issue on 18 Nov and mitigated it on 19 Nov; instances not configured to its recommended practices exposed management functions to an unauthorised party. Possibly exposed: secrets in Named Values, identity-provider and OpenID Connect client secrets, subscription keys and management tokens. Norwegian authorities link the flaw to attacks on energy companies (SecurityWeek).

deck.headline: RBI proposes a 'stop switch' and widens when banks must pay for digital fraud
deck.summary: India's central bank proposes letting customers switch off digital payment channels, cap transactions and add a trusted second approver for large transfers. Banks that fail to offer these, or miss alerts and complaints, would be treated as negligent and bear fraud losses. Comments are due by 14 December.
deck.whyItMatters: Indian banks would need to build channel kill-switches and a delegated-approval flow, and would carry more fraud losses where they fall short; product, fraud and legal teams should respond before 14 Dec.
deck.storyline: Storyline: how India's RBI supervises banks · day 6
deck.detailHtml: The Reserve Bank of India published draft amendments on 23 Nov to its responsible-business-conduct rules for every kind of bank, from commercial and small finance banks to co-operatives. Customers would get customer-induced controls, a so-called stop switch: the option to disable digital payment channels, set transaction limits and block future debits. A Trusted Person Mechanism would add an extra approval for transfers above a threshold the customer sets (ET BFSI). The RBI also widens what counts as bank negligence in fraudulent electronic transactions, which decides who bears the loss: not offering these controls, not applying required authentication, not sending alerts, delaying complaints, system malfunctions, security breaches and collusion by staff or third parties. It builds on June's customer-liability rules. Comments are due by 14 Dec. The same day the RBI kept SBI (0.80% extra CET1), HDFC Bank (0.40%) and ICICI Bank (0.20%) as systemically important banks.

deck.headline: China's Z.ai ships GLM-5.4, a 750B model that runs half its layers twice
deck.summary: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 is a 750-billion-parameter model that runs half its layers twice per token, a 'looped' design that adds depth without adding weights. Z.ai claims it matches models of 2-3 trillion parameters. It is on Z.ai's coding plan now, with open weights promised. Benchmarks are the company's own.
deck.whyItMatters: Two looped models in four days, one at frontier scale, suggest 'more compute per token' is becoming a standard way to get bigger-model quality from smaller weights; if the weights ship, expect it to undercut US closed models on price.
deck.storyline: Storyline: new kinds of AI models · day 11
deck.detailHtml: Z.ai (Zhipu) launched GLM-5.4 on 23 Nov, its first loop transformer: instead of using each layer once, the 750B-parameter model runs a block of shared layers (27 to 54) twice, making the network deeper without adding parameters. Z.ai retrained the GLM-5 base into a loop model, saying loop models trained from scratch did worse; per-token gates control how much each pass changes the result, and both passes share the KV cache so a 1M-token context stays affordable (The Decoder). Z.ai claims it performs like models of 2-3 trillion parameters and runs at 70-200 tokens a second. In a matched 30B test, looping lifted AIME25 from 19.2 to 30.4 with about 10% more training compute. It is on Z.ai's Coding Plan (not yet the regular API); weights are promised. Simon Willison found it comparable in quality to OpenAI and Anthropic models on his informal tests. It follows Thinking Machines' looped Inkling 2 Mini (20 Nov).

deck.headline: Nasdaq jumps 6.5% and Nvidia 31% as Huang's return ends the sell-off streak
deck.summary: Wall Street recovered most of Friday's losses on Monday. The Nasdaq rose 6.5%, the S&P 500 4.7% and Nvidia 31.5% to $165.05 after Jensen Huang's reinstatement, adding about $1tn to its value. Micron and Tesla also jumped. Anthropic was an exception, slipping 1.4% to $87.64.
deck.whyItMatters: One personnel decision moved US equities by trillions in a day, which shows how concentrated AI risk has become; risk teams should treat single-name events at Nvidia as market-wide shocks in stress tests.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI stocks and market mood · day 4
deck.detailHtml: Markets reversed Friday's rout on Monday 23 Nov. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 24,089.56, up 6.5%; the S&P 500 rose 4.7% to 7,237.17 and the Dow 3.0% to 49,595.31 (market data). Nvidia jumped 31.5% to $165.05, adding close to $1tn in value, though it is still about 21% below a month ago (BBC). Micron rose 19%, Tesla 11.5% and AMD about 7%; Apple and Microsoft gained under 2%. The BBC says the rally began before the announcement and ended a week-long losing streak. Anthropic bucked it, slipping 1.4% to $87.64, close to its $83 IPO price. The US 10-year yield was flat at 4.92%. Asia followed on Tuesday: the Nikkei rose about 4% and the Kospi about 2.5%. Bitcoin touched $64,505 before easing to about $61,200 (Cointelegraph; market data).

deck.headline: US banks shift AI-agent risk to customers as Wells Fargo's new terms start
deck.summary: Wells Fargo's new customer terms, live from 24 November, say any AI agent use is at the customer's own risk. Major US banks are blocking third-party bots from logging in and shifting liability for bot mistakes to customers. Reuters reports some banks are tightening agent controls further.
deck.whyItMatters: The industry default is becoming 'block outside agents, push liability to the customer'; banks that want agent traffic will need an approved channel (scoped tokens, limits, logs) rather than screen-scraping logins.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI agents and financial firms · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Wells Fargo's updated agreement with millions of customers takes effect on 24 Nov and says: 'Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK.' WIRED (22 Nov) reports that major US banks are banning third-party bots from logging into customer accounts and warning that costly bot mistakes are the customer's problem; Citi changed its terms in the same way last week. On 23 Nov Reuters reported, as an exclusive, that some US banks are tightening controls on AI agents over concern that models can escape safeguards (headline seen; article not opened). The moves follow Arizona's criminal probe into 'rogue AI agents' in banks (edition 149).

deck.headline: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents review, fix and approve code changes
deck.summary: Anthropic's new Claude Ship, in beta, reviews pull requests, pushes fixes and can approve changes that a team's own policy allows, so routine code can merge without a human sign-off. Teams choose which changes still need a person. Enterprise customers can claim at least $10,000 in credits.
deck.whyItMatters: Letting an AI approve its own kind of code moves accountability out of the four-eyes principle banks rely on; change-management and audit teams should decide now which change classes, if any, may be agent-approved.
deck.storyline: Storyline: tools for AI coding agents · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta on 23 Nov. It reviews pull requests, pushes fixes and approves the changes a team's policy allows, so routine changes can merge without a human approver; teams decide where it runs and which changes still need a person. Anthropic says that on the Claude Code team 'Claude writes most of our code' and it wanted everything after the PR to move as fast. Eligible Claude Enterprise organisations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits. TechCrunch notes that automatic approval, not review, is the new part: code review tools already existed.

deck.headline: US moves to blacklist Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer at the centre of the spy scandal
deck.summary: The US Commerce Department will put Singapore's Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer whose former CEO is alleged to be a Chinese spy, on its trade blacklist. Commerce says it spent almost two years investigating whether the firm moved Nvidia chips into China. No start date was given.
deck.whyItMatters: The listing lands the same day Huang returns, so the export-control story continues even as the leadership one closes; banks financing Asian GPU clouds should screen for Megaspeed links and expect tighter end-use checks.
deck.storyline: Storyline: who can buy top AI chips · day 14
deck.detailHtml: The US Commerce Department announced on 23 Nov that it plans to add Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-centre developer and Nvidia customer, to its Entity List, which bars US trade without a licence (BBC). Commerce says it had investigated for almost two years whether Megaspeed helped move Nvidia's advanced chips to Chinese companies; it gave no effective date. Megaspeed's former CEO Alice Huang is alleged by US officials to be a Chinese intelligence asset who had an affair with Jensen Huang; China denies it and warns against a 'technological blockade'. Politicians have criticised Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not listing the company earlier (DW).
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBBC: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal · DW: US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist

deck.headline: COP31 climate talks end without a final agreement for the first time since 2009
deck.summary: The UN climate summit in Antalya ended on Sunday without its usual final statement, the first time since 2009. Countries split over mentioning fossil fuels and over money for poorer nations; the EU and others rejected the text. Smaller decisions on worker transition and adaptation did pass.
deck.whyItMatters: With no new global signal, climate policy moves back to national rules and trade measures such as the EU's carbon border tax; banks' transition plans should assume slower, more fragmented regulation.
deck.detailHtml: The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday 22 Nov without consensus on a cover decision, the summit's main statement, for the first time since 2009 (Inside Climate News via Ars Technica). Countries split over whether to mention fossil fuels and carbon capture and over how much climate finance rich countries should provide; the EU, several Latin American countries and Pacific island states refused the presidency's text. Some decisions passed, including a programme to help workers and communities move away from fossil fuels and a plan to assess adaptation progress. A push for voluntary global electrification goals failed. More than 100,000 people attended.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGArs Technica / Inside Climate News: COP31 ends in failure · BBC: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks

deck.headline: Ukrainian drones sink a Russian warship in a Libyan port, far from the front
deck.summary: Ukraine says seven naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya, and hit a Russian cargo ship it says carried weapons. Both of Libya's rival governments condemned the strike and the Kremlin warned of escalation. Marine insurers are widening war-risk zones.
deck.whyItMatters: Ukraine can now strike Russian assets in the Mediterranean, which raises war-risk premiums and sanctions-screening stakes for shipping finance and trade-finance desks.
deck.storyline: Storyline: the war in Ukraine · day 4
deck.detailHtml: A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at the Benghazi naval base in Libya on Sunday 22 Nov, President Zelensky said; he named the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, and said seven naval drones were used. Ukraine says it also hit a Russian cargo ship it accuses of carrying weapons. Libya's rival governments in Tripoli and Benghazi both condemned the attack; the Kremlin warned of 'escalation of tensions in the region' (BBC). Insurance Business reports the strike widens the war-risk area for Mediterranean shipping. Zelensky has since called for four-way peace talks with Russia, Europe and the US.

deck.headline: Amazon buys Decart's inference-optimisation tech and team to speed up Trainium
deck.summary: Amazon is buying the technology behind Decart's optimisation stack and hiring its founders and team to make inference on its Trainium chips faster and cheaper. Decart has worked with Amazon since 2025. Reports put the price at $7.5bn; Amazon did not disclose one.
deck.whyItMatters: The cost of AI is increasingly set by software that squeezes chips, not just the chips; cheaper Trainium inference strengthens AWS's pitch to banks weighing Nvidia-based clouds.
deck.storyline: Storyline: Big Tech's own AI chips · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Amazon said on 23 Nov it has agreed to buy the proprietary technology behind the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS) and bring Decart's co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf, with their researchers and engineers, to Amazon. Decart has worked with Amazon since 2025 on getting more performance out of Trainium by tuning software and hardware together; Amazon says the deal will speed inference and its custom chips for language, multimodal, agent and world models. Tech in Asia and others report the price at $7.5bn; Amazon did not state one. Decart is known for real-time world models such as Oasis.

deck.headline: DeepMind's Gemini agents find cheaper quantum algorithms and prove them in Lean
deck.summary: Google DeepMind says teams of Gemini 4 agents found cheaper quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems and proved each one correct in Lean. One fusion calculation became 11.8 times cheaper; a common maths routine more than 290 times cheaper. No quantum computer can run them yet.
deck.whyItMatters: AI that makes quantum algorithms cheaper pulls forward the date when quantum machines matter, including for breaking today's encryption; keep post-quantum migration plans on schedule.
deck.detailHtml: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI said on 23 Nov that teams of Gemini 4 agents found more efficient quantum algorithms for problems in fusion, chemistry and drug design, and proved each result correct in the Lean theorem prover, because the circuits are too big to test on any computer today. The biggest gain: an 11.8x cheaper calculation for laser-driven fusion fuel, with memory down from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits. A light-sensitive molecule simulation became about 8x cheaper, the enzyme cytochrome P450 2.5x, and a widely used maths routine more than 290x (TNW). Agent teams shared verified ideas in a common notebook and 'met' every four hours to compare approaches.

deck.headline: OpenAI and Cisco open-source Shirudo to shield unpatched Linux servers with AI
deck.summary: OpenAI and Cisco released Shirudo, open-source software that lets AI agents write small in-kernel rules to block an exploit on a running Linux server until a patch is ready. In OpenAI's test, a Codex-written shield stopped a Java4Shell attack on live Elasticsearch without a restart.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks often wait weeks to patch core Linux systems; an open, auditable stop-gap layer is worth piloting, but treat agent-written kernel rules as code that needs review.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI used to defend computer systems · day 2
deck.detailHtml: OpenAI and Cisco launched Shirudo on 23 Nov, an open-source runtime that protects Linux systems while patches are tested and rolled out. It uses eBPF, small programs that run inside the operating system, to block the specific code path an exploit needs without taking the service offline. Agents can investigate a vulnerability, write a targeted 'shield' and test it against exploits and real traffic; security teams decide what is enforced and can watch a shield's effect before turning it on. In a controlled test a Codex-written shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service with no restart, OpenAI says.

deck.headline: CFTC staff let exchanges count bitcoin and ether toward required reserves
deck.summary: Staff at the US derivatives regulator say exchanges and clearinghouses can count some crypto, reportedly including bitcoin, ether and stablecoins, toward the reserves they must hold to cover operating costs, but not toward their separate liquidity requirement. It is a staff advisory, not a formal rule.
deck.whyItMatters: It lets crypto-native venues use their own holdings to meet capital-like tests, which makes them more viable as regulated counterparties; banks clearing through them should check how much of a venue's cushion is now volatile crypto.
deck.storyline: Storyline: who runs US crypto regulation · day 4
deck.detailHtml: Staff at the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in an advisory on 23 Nov that some crypto assets can count toward the financial resources that trading platforms and clearinghouses must hold to cover operating costs, but not toward a separate liquidity requirement (Reuters via CNA). It applies to swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organisations. Cointelegraph and The Block say bitcoin, ether and stablecoins are covered. It is a staff advisory, not a rule.

deck.headline: Medicare's third round of drug-price talks to save $9.2bn, first with clinic drugs
deck.summary: Medicare says its third round of drug-price negotiations will save $9.2bn next year, 45% less than last year's prices would have cost. For the first time it covers drugs given in doctors' offices, not just pharmacy drugs. The figure leaves out discounts drugmakers already pay.
deck.whyItMatters: Negotiated prices now reach infusion and specialist drugs, which hits the revenue models of large drugmakers and the lenders and investors exposed to them.
deck.storyline: Storyline: what the US pays for medicines · day 2
deck.detailHtml: The Trump administration said on 23 Nov that Medicare will save $9.2bn on drugs next year from its third round of price negotiations, a net saving of 45% against what it would have paid at last year's prices (STAT). It is the first round to include Part B drugs, given in doctors' offices, alongside retail Part D drugs. The estimate excludes discounts drugmakers already pay through the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program, which would shrink the figure.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGSTAT: Medicare estimates $9.2 billion in savings from third round of negotiated drug prices

deck.headline: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX over Grok-made sexual deepfakes, including of children
deck.summary: Virginia and Oregon sued SpaceX, which owns xAI, alleging its Grok chatbot made nude deepfakes of millions of people earlier this year, including children, and that weak safeguards were a selling point. The states use consumer-protection law and want a court to stop such images.
deck.whyItMatters: State consumer-protection law is becoming the route to hold AI makers liable for outputs; firms deploying image models need provable abuse filters, not policy statements.
deck.detailHtml: The attorneys general of Virginia (Jay Jones) and Oregon (Dan Rayfield) filed lawsuits on 23 Nov accusing SpaceX, which now owns xAI, and its subsidiaries of breaking state consumer and trade laws by letting Grok make deepfake nude images of millions of people earlier this year, including sexual images of children (CyberScoop). They allege SpaceX and Elon Musk repeatedly failed to block the nudification feature and that weak safeguards were a selling point to set Grok apart. Ars Technica says the states want a court order stopping Grok from generating such images.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGCyberScoop: Virginia, Oregon hit SpaceX with fresh lawsuits over Grok-created CSAM · Ars Technica: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images

alsoToday.summary: Apple is adding Tap to Share, an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone: a shopper taps a merchant's iPhone to share email, shipping address and loyalty details and watch the basket update before paying with Apple Pay.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Walmart's switch removes the last big US holdout against tap-to-pay wallets; debit top-ups inside Wallet put Apple between banks and their cardholders.

alsoToday.summary: Genworth's CareScout unit has stopped writing new long-term care insurance, ThinkAdvisor and Insurance Business report. CEO Tom McInerney left early, effective 19 Nov, citing his health; CFO Jerome Upton is confirmed as president and CEO, and Angela Simmons is due to become CFO on 1 Jan 2027.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: One of the last US long-term care writers is pulling back, leaving fewer ways to insure care costs that banks' wealth clients increasingly ask about.

alsoToday.headline: India's Sarvam releases an upgraded open 105B model and defends hosting Chinese AI
alsoToday.summary: Bengaluru's Sarvam AI released an upgraded 105B model with open weights in BF16 and NVFP4; it says the 65GB NVFP4 version runs on a single Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU (Analytics India Magazine, 23 Nov).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: An Indian open model that fits on one workstation GPU is a practical option for banks needing on-premises AI under data-localisation rules.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Bengaluru's Sarvam AI released an upgraded 105B model with open weights in BF16 and NVFP4; it says the 65GB NVFP4 version runs on a single Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU (Analytics India Magazine, 23 Nov). Its results are from its own evaluations; Gemini scored higher on some tests. Sarvam also defended hosting Chinese models on its token service, saying its own models remain the core focus, and plans vision, speech and edge models over the next two weeks.

alsoToday.headline: Ladybird, the first new independent browser engine in years, reaches alpha
alsoToday.summary: Ladybird, a browser whose engine is written from the ground up rather than forked from Chromium, WebKit or Gecko, released its first alpha for macOS and Linux on 23 Nov, founder Andreas Kling wrote. It is a rolling channel with automatic updates; some sites will break and it makes no security promises yet.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A fourth engine matters for web resilience; web teams can start adding it to test matrices.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: alternatives to Big Tech apps · day 2

alsoToday.headline: FDA approves BridgeBio's Welgemda, the first drug for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
alsoToday.summary: The FDA approved BridgeBio's Welgemda on 23 Nov, the first approved treatment for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, a group of inherited muscle-wasting diseases, according to STAT, Endpoints and Seeking Alpha. Details of the label were not available in what we could open.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Another rare-disease first, days after the FDA rejected Capricor's Duchenne therapy.

alsoToday.headline: South Korea's education minister quits over AI cheating on the college entrance exam
alsoToday.summary: South Korea's education minister has resigned over the government's rules against AI-assisted cheating on the CSAT university entrance exam, The New York Times reports (22 Nov). On 16 Nov he told the National Assembly the ministry could not guarantee detecting cheating with AI devices such as smart glasses, and a complaint accusing him of dereliction of duty followed (Korea Herald).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Wearable AI is breaking high-stakes testing, including the professional exams banks rely on for certification.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: AI and cheating in exams · day 2
alsoToday.detailHtml: South Korea's education minister has resigned over the government's rules against AI-assisted cheating on the CSAT university entrance exam, The New York Times reports (22 Nov). On 16 Nov he told the National Assembly the ministry could not guarantee detecting cheating with AI devices such as smart glasses, and a complaint accusing him of dereliction of duty followed (Korea Herald). The ministry had already banned AI glasses and promised criminal charges and a three-year exam ban for offenders.

alsoToday.headline: Verstappen wins a record-overtake Las Vegas Grand Prix from Norris
alsoToday.summary: Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Saturday night by 0.639s from McLaren's Lando Norris, his third Las Vegas win in four years, with Oscar Piastri third (Reuters via CNA). Formula One said the 50-lap race had 352 overtakes and 35 lead changes, driven by energy deployment and overtaking modes on the long straights, in front of a sold-out crowd…
alsoToday.whyItMatters: The new energy rules are producing races fans like, which helps F1's US commercial push.

alsoToday.headline: Allstate silent on reports of about 5,000 job cuts tied to AI
alsoToday.summary: Crain's Chicago Business reports that Allstate is staying silent on reports that it will cut about 5,000 jobs as it uses more AI; earlier trade reports citing unnamed sources said up to 10% of its roughly 53,000 staff could be affected.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: If confirmed, one of the largest AI-linked white-collar cuts in insurance; watch for a WARN notice or an Allstate statement.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Crain's Chicago Business reports that Allstate is staying silent on reports that it will cut about 5,000 jobs as it uses more AI; earlier trade reports citing unnamed sources said up to 10% of its roughly 53,000 staff could be affected. Allstate has said it used AI to write over 12 million lines of code in the third quarter. The company has not confirmed any cuts.
